engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Strategy: Weak Squares
chess.body: A weak square is one that cannot be defended by a pawn. d5 is weak for Black if the c6 and e6 pawns are gone or never played. Plant a knight on a weak square — it becomes an 'outpost.' From d5, a knight controls 8 squares and cannot be chased. Outpost knight + weak squares = long-term advantage.

book.author: Sam Walton
book.lesson: Sam Walton built the world's largest retailer from a small Arkansas five-and-dime store. His rules: commit to your business; share profits with employees; energise your associates; communicate everything; appreciate associates; celebrate successes; listen to everyone in your company; exceed customers' expectations; control expenses; swim upstream (do the opposite of what everyone else does). The most counterintuitive: Walmart succeeded by treating employees as partners and sharing information and profits broadly, while competitors treated labour as a cost to minimise. Also: Walton flew his own plane to personally visit stores until he was 70.
book.key_quote: The best business intelligence comes from people closest to the customer. Go there yourself and listen.
book.action: Identify someone in your team or organisation who is closest to the customer/problem. Ask them what they're seeing that leadership doesn't know about.
crux: Walton's obsession was the customer's price, and everything else followed from it.
Buy low, stack it high, sell it cheap. Volume compensates for margin.
Rural small towns were dismissed by competitors. That was the opening.
Control costs better than anyone. Cost advantage forgives many mistakes.
Distribution centres came before the stores they served. Logistics was the real business.
Invest early in information systems. Walmart's data infrastructure preceded everyone's.
Share profits with associates and they behave like owners.
Listen to the people on the floor. They talk to customers; you don't.
Swim upstream. Go the other way when everyone agrees.
Every store must be visited. Management by walking around, constantly.
Copy shamelessly from competitors. Walton toured rivals' stores relentlessly.
Exceed expectations, celebrate success, and keep the culture unembarrassed.
Frugality is cultural, not cosmetic — shared hotel rooms while running a Fortune 500 company.
learnings: A cost advantage is a strategy, not an accounting detail.
Infrastructure before expansion, or expansion breaks you.
Frontline staff hold the information leadership needs.
Copying well is faster than inventing badly.
examples: Walmart's hub-and-spoke DCs let it saturate regions competitors couldn't serve profitably.
Walton flew his own plane over towns scouting sites, personally, for years.
Profit-sharing from 1971 turned shelf-stackers into shareholders and cut shrinkage.
adapt: Your cost advantage is the whole stack running on GitHub Actions and Vercel free tiers. Protect it.
Infrastructure before features: fix the position lifecycle before adding another scanner.
Copy shamelessly — study what the good finance pages do, then do it in your voice.
Swim upstream: everyone posts motivational finance. Post the actual numbers, including the losses.

minimalism.title: The 90/90 Rule
minimalism.body: Have you used it in the last 90 days? Will you in the next 90? If both answers are no, it is storage, not ownership. You are paying rent on it in square feet and attention.

interview_tech.q: What is the difference between an associate and a subsidiary in your accounts?
interview_tech.a: Control versus significant influence. A subsidiary is controlled — you consolidate line by line and recognise NCI. An associate is significant influence, presumed at 20–50%, accounted for using the equity method: one line on the balance sheet at cost plus your share of post-acquisition reserves, and one line in P&L for your share of profit. Nothing of the associate's revenue or EBITDA enters your group numbers — a point that catches people out when a joint-venture-heavy group reports headline growth.

interview_tech.q: Compare owned retail, franchise, and concession from a finance perspective.
interview_tech.a: Owned: full revenue, full margin, full capex, full lease and staffing risk. Franchise: you book a royalty and wholesale margin — far lower revenue, far lower risk, and no control over the customer experience. Concession: you occupy space inside a host retailer, pay a percentage of sales rather than fixed rent, so occupancy cost flexes with trading and downside is capped. In the Gulf, franchise is the dominant international-brand model, which is why groups like Alshaya and Al-Futtaim report differently from the brands they carry.

interview_soft.q: What do you know about our company?
interview_soft.a: The disqualifying answer is anything from the homepage. Come with: their last reported results and one number from them, their format or brand mix and how it differs from peers, one strategic move in the last 18 months, and one question you genuinely cannot answer from outside. For a Gulf retail group that means knowing their franchise portfolio, which markets they operate directly versus through partners, and their exposure to mall footfall.

interview_soft.q: How do you build credibility in the first 90 days in a new company?
interview_soft.a: Deliver one visible thing early and be accurate about everything. Concretely: get the close done cleanly, learn the actual business by walking the stores rather than reading the reports, and find the one number everyone argues about and fix its definition. Do not restructure anything in the first quarter. Credibility in finance is cumulative and fragile — it comes from being right repeatedly, not from an early bold move.

cfo_field.q: Explain a variance in one sentence or you do not understand it yet.
cfo_field.a: 'Margin is down 180bps: 120 from promotional depth in electronics, 40 from freight, 20 mix.' That is a CFO answer. A table of forty lines is a controller answer. The discipline is to decompose until the drivers are additive and then name the largest two. If you cannot make the bridge add up, you have a data problem, not a communication problem.

cfo_field.q: Working capital is where a retail CFO is actually judged.
cfo_field.a: EBITDA gets the headline; the cash conversion cycle gets the board's attention. DIO + DSO − DPO. Retail is inventory-heavy and often near-zero DSO, so the fight is DIO against DPO. Cutting DIO from 95 to 80 days on AED 400M COGS releases roughly AED 16.4M of cash — permanently, without selling a single extra unit. That is a bigger number than most cost programmes deliver, and it does not need a headcount conversation.
